title: Requirements Analysis and Relational Schema Planning
learningObjectives: Translate a small business requirement into entities and relationships.
Choose primary and foreign keys for related tables.
Represent one-to-many relationships without repeating parent data.
Use constraints to encode required fields and valid states.
Verify the schema with a practical join and grouped report.

understand.concept: Requirements analysis identifies the people, events, rules and reports a database must support. The schema turns those requirements into entities, keys, relationships and constraints.
understand.whyItMatters: Starting with a clear data model reduces duplicated data and prevents missing relationships from being patched into queries later.
understand.analogy: A building plan identifies rooms, doors and load-bearing walls before construction begins.
understand.analogyLimit: A relational schema does not capture every workflow rule; some requirements belong in application logic, triggers or operational processes.

explain.narrative:
## Start from the business questions
For a service desk, the system must identify customers, record support tickets, track ticket status and priority, and report open work by customer. Those requirements suggest separate customer and ticket entities.

## Model relationships
One customer can open many tickets, so tickets store customer_id as a foreign key. Customer name and contact details remain in the customer table rather than being repeated on every ticket.

## Encode invariants
Use NOT NULL for required values, UNIQUE for stable business identifiers, CHECK for controlled states and FOREIGN KEY for relationships. Enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement on each connection.

## Validate against real questions
After creating the schema, insert representative data and write the joins and reports the application needs. If a required report is awkward or duplicates data, revisit the model before adding more columns.

examples.title: Create customer and support-ticket entities
examples.code: CREATE TABLE prj24_customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); CREATE TABLE prj24_tickets (ticket_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES prj24_customers(customer_id), subject TEXT NOT NULL, priority INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 5), status TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('open','in_progress','closed')));
examples.explanation: Creates two entities and a one-to-many relationship. Customer details are stored once; each ticket references its customer through a foreign key.

examples.title: Insert customers and representative tickets
examples.code: INSERT INTO prj24_customers VALUES (1, 'Asha', 'asha@example.test'), (2, 'Bilal', 'bilal@example.test'); INSERT INTO prj24_tickets VALUES (101, 1, 'Cannot sign in', 5, 'open'), (102, 1, 'Invoice question', 2, 'in_progress'), (103, 2, 'App is slow', 4, 'open');
examples.explanation: Adds two customers and three tickets. The data covers two priorities and two statuses for reporting practice.

examples.title: List open tickets with their customer
examples.code: SELECT t.ticket_id, c.customer_name, t.subject, t.priority FROM prj24_tickets AS t JOIN prj24_customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.status = 'open' ORDER BY t.priority DESC, t.ticket_id;
examples.expectedOutput: 101 | Asha | Cannot sign in | 5; 103 | Bilal | App is slow | 4
examples.explanation: Joins ticket events to customer details and filters open work. The ticket_id tie-breaker keeps the report deterministic.

examples.title: Count tickets by status
examples.code: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS ticket_count FROM prj24_tickets GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;
examples.explanation: Groups the three ticket rows by status. Because no closed row exists, no closed group is returned; the result contains only statuses present in the data.

examples.title: Close one ticket and verify the new state
examples.code: UPDATE prj24_tickets SET status = 'closed' WHERE ticket_id = 101; SELECT ticket_id, status FROM prj24_tickets WHERE ticket_id = 101;
examples.explanation: Updates one ticket using its primary key and verifies the resulting state. Production code should check that exactly one row was updated.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and draw the customer-to-ticket relationship. Explain why customer_name belongs in the customer table rather than being copied into every ticket row.
practise.independentTask: Extend the model with ticket_comments. Define its primary key, foreign key, required fields and a query that returns each ticket with its latest comment.
hints: Start from required business questions and reports.
Separate entities that have independent identity.
Use foreign keys for one-to-many relationships.
Use CHECK for controlled states and ranges.
Test the schema with representative joins and reports.

questions.prompt: What should requirements analysis identify first?
options: Business entities, rules and required reports
Only the preferred SQL keyword case
Only the number of indexes
Only the UI colour scheme
questions.answer: Business entities, rules and required reports
questions.explanation: The schema should be driven by data needs and business questions.

questions.prompt: How is a one-to-many customer-ticket relationship represented?
options: Store customer_id as a foreign key in tickets
Copy the customer row into every ticket
Store all ticket IDs in one text field
Use a CROSS JOIN
questions.answer: Store customer_id as a foreign key in tickets
questions.explanation: Each ticket references one customer; a customer can have many tickets.

questions.prompt: Why use a UNIQUE constraint on email?
options: To prevent duplicate email values in the table
To sort email values
To encrypt email values
To create a backup
questions.answer: To prevent duplicate email values in the table
questions.explanation: UNIQUE enforces a uniqueness rule on stored values.

questions.prompt: What does CHECK(priority BETWEEN 1 AND 5) enforce?
options: Priority values must be within the allowed range
Every ticket must be closed
Each customer must have five tickets
Priority must be text
questions.answer: Priority values must be within the allowed range
questions.explanation: CHECK validates the row expression when data is written.

questions.prompt: Why verify a schema with joins and reports?
options: To confirm it supports real application questions correctly
To avoid creating primary keys
To remove all constraints
To make every query return one row
questions.answer: To confirm it supports real application questions correctly
questions.explanation: A design must support its intended reads and relationships.
